problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown function $f(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ f(t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}
$$

*Hint: One of the eigenvalues of the matrix is ${\lambda }_{1}=4+\text{i}.$*

examples.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/471ff0aa856363c49a494f0e711dec8558b429261ddd99685bd0a19416264d05.png) 

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda_1=1+\textrm{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For $\lambda_1 =1+\textrm{i},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/9fbccda402b330b568828c47040f1867c0b075ff434f6d94c2d5d5bcea85f4a8.png)
So, we get an eigenvector 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/91e10c00aed02305fdb5afd421aad57fe52143e3305d84da00819e62f2b30a14.png)

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue $\lambda_2 = \overline{\lambda}_1$ is 
$\mathbf{v}_2 = \overline{\mathbf{v}}_1.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue $\lambda_1 = 1+\textrm{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/2ccc9c4cb7dd95e168690c017e8fca6f92315d1759b3e3ec6bb3a82551b39e3c.png)

We now separate this solution into its real and imaginary parts. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(1+\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i}({e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\text{ } \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}({e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $\mathbf w_1$ and $\mathbf w_2$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t) = \cos{t}.$

feedback.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
feedback.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].$

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}](\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\text{i}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =3[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
